situationBrief.title: Revisiting the School Archive Timeline
situationBrief.description: Class 10 students are editing the annual school archive. Earlier events, unfinished durations, sequence of tenses, and five ways of expressing future time need careful repair.

beats.speaker: mira
beats.actionLabel: Reads two past events in one sentence
beats.dialogue: Look at this archive sentence: 'When we reached the hall, the science quiz already started.' Two past actions happened—which one happened FIRST?

beats.speaker: arjun
beats.actionLabel: Checks reported statements and future plans
beats.dialogue: And look at the next slip: 'Our teacher said that the earth moved round the sun.' Wait—does the earth still move round the sun today?
beats.cardPreviewText: When we reached the hall, the quiz had started.

beats.speaker: gyan
beats.dialogue: In Class 10, we master how Past Simple differs from Present Perfect and Past Perfect ('earlier past'), how Sequence of Tenses handles universal truths, and how five future forms express plans, timetables, and predictions!

grammarOutcomes: Select accurately among the 6 ways of expressing Past Time—especially Past Simple vs Present Perfect and Past Perfect for an earlier past event.
Apply Sequence of Tenses across main and subordinate clauses, including the universal-truth exception.
Choose purposefully among future-time forms ('will', 'be going to', Present Progressive, Present Simple timetable, and 'will have + V3').
learningObjectives.knowledgeOutcome: Audit Indian school archives, ISRO science talks, railway timetables, and community eco-drives with precision.

sourceReferences.bookTitle: Learn and Practise Grammar Class - X
sourceReferences.note: Consolidates the 2-tense + 3-time model, Present Time, 6 ways of expressing Past Time (including Past Perfect for earlier past and Present Perfect with 'for/since'), and 5 ways of expressing Future Time.

sourceReferences.bookTitle: A NEW METHOD English Grammar For Class IX & X
sourceReferences.note: Combined Classes IX & X resource teaching 3-Tense / 12-sub-tense labels, stative non-continuous verbs, 'for/since', and 15 common tense error corrections.

sourceReferences.bookTitle: A Practice Book of ENGLISH GRAMMAR & COMPOSITION (GRAMMAR IN USE) for Class IX
sourceReferences.chapter: Chapter 9 Sec. 1 & 3: Use of Tenses & Sequence of Tenses
sourceReferences.note: Cross-board reference for Sequence of Tenses and universal-truth exception (Note: no Class 10 PSEB textbook was supplied among sources).
Synthesises Odisha X Tense Revisited with Assam IX-X and notes explicitly that PSEB Class X was not supplied.

sentences.title: Earlier Past Event
sentences.rawText: When we reached the hall, the quiz had already begun.
sentences.note: Past Perfect ('had + V3') marks the action that happened BEFORE another past action ('reached').

tokens.meaningInSentence: Links two past actions in sequence.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Introduces the later past event 'we reached'.
Past Simple marks the point in the past after the quiz started.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the event that began first.
Pushes the action further back in past time.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: 'had + begun' expresses the earlier of two past events.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Shows the first action was complete before arrival.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Past participle of begin (begin / began / begun).

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: When two actions happen in the past, the earlier one takes Past Perfect ('had begun') and the later one takes Past Simple ('reached').

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'the quiz' is the main clause Subject.
groups.textbookRule: Past Perfect is used for the earlier of two past actions (Odisha X Ch. 1 p. 6; PSEB IX p. 96; Assam p. 142).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.plainExplanation: 'had already begun' happened before 'we reached the hall'.
groups.textbookRule: Earlier past = had + V3; later past = V2.

relationships.label: reached ↔ had begun
relationships.explanation: 'had begun' occurred earlier in the past than 'reached'.

structureSummary.predicateText: had already begun (when we reached the hall)
structureSummary.patternNote: Two past events → Earlier: Past Perfect ('had begun'), Later: Past Simple ('reached').

sentences.title: Action Continuing Until Now
sentences.rawText: Dr. Nair has taught physics here for twelve years.
sentences.note: Present Perfect ('has/have + V3') or Present Perfect Progressive covers duration up to now with 'for' or 'since'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Anchors the period up to today.
Expresses teaching across twelve years until today.

verbMeta.timeCommunicated: Past Starting Point Continuing to Present
verbMeta.whyAppropriate: 'for twelve years' marks a duration continuing into the present—Past Simple ('taught') would imply he stopped, and Present Simple ('teaches') ignores the 12-year span.

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Use 'for' + length of time (twelve years); use 'since' + starting point (2014).

groups.label: Subject
groups.textbookRule: Present Perfect / Present Perfect Progressive links a past start to the present via 'for' (period) or 'since' (point) (Odisha X pp. 4-5; Assam pp. 139-140).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.questionPrompt: How long has he taught here?
groups.plainExplanation: 'has taught ... for twelve years' connects 12 years ago to today.
groups.textbookRule: Avoid 'is teaching here for twelve years'.

relationships.label: for twelve years → has taught
relationships.explanation: 'for twelve years' calls for Present Perfect ('has taught') or Present Perfect Progressive ('has been teaching').

structureSummary.predicateText: has taught physics here for twelve years
structureSummary.patternNote: Length of time continuing to now ('for twelve years') → Present Perfect.

sentences.title: Sequence of Tenses Exception
sentences.rawText: Our teacher explained that the earth moves round the sun.
sentences.note: Although 'explained' is Past Simple, the reported fact stays Present Simple ('moves') because it is always true.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Shows the explanation happened in the past.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Normally triggers past in subordinate clause—except for universal truths!

tokens.meaningInSentence: Expresses a scientific fact true past, present, and future.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Universal truths keep Present Simple even after a past main verb.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: Even though 'explained' is Past, scientific laws and universal truths keep Present Simple ('moves').

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the star at the centre.

groups.label: Subject
groups.textbookRule: Under Sequence of Tenses, a universal truth or habitual fact stays in Present Simple even when the reporting verb is Past (PSEB IX p. 101).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.questionPrompt: Why does 'moves' stay in Present Simple?
groups.plainExplanation: Because Earth still orbits the sun—universal truths do not shift to Past.

relationships.label: moves ← earth
relationships.explanation: 'moves' keeps Present Simple for a timeless scientific truth.

structureSummary.predicateText: explained that the earth moves round the sun
structureSummary.patternNote: Past reporting verb + Universal truth → Present Simple ('moves').

sentences.title: Five Ways to Express Future Time
sentences.rawText: By 5 p.m., the volunteers will have sorted all the books.
sentences.note: Future Perfect ('will have + V3') shows an action completed BEFORE a set future deadline ('By 5 p.m.').

tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: 'By + future time' commonly cues Future Perfect.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Shows sorting will be finished by 5 p.m.

verbMeta.whyAppropriate: 'By 5 p.m.' highlights that the work will be finished before that clock time.

groups.label: Subject
groups.textbookRule: Odisha X Ch. 1 (pp. 8-12) teaches 5 ways of expressing future time, including 'will have + V3' for completion before a future deadline.

groups.label: Predicate
groups.questionPrompt: What will be finished by 5 p.m.?
groups.plainExplanation: 'will have sorted all the books' shows future completion.
groups.textbookRule: Future deadline ('By 5 p.m.') + completion → 'will have + V3'.

relationships.label: By 5 p.m. → will have sorted
relationships.explanation: 'By 5 p.m.' marks a deadline before which sorting finishes.

structureSummary.predicateText: By 5 p.m., ... will have sorted all the books

teachingSequence.title: Two Events in the Past
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: When two actions happen in the past, which happened first?
teachingSequence.explanation: Odisha Class X 'Tense Revisited' highlights 6 ways to express Past Time. When one past event ('the quiz began') finished BEFORE another past event ('we reached the hall'), use Past Perfect ('had begun') for the earlier event and Past Simple ('reached') for the later one.

timelineData.grammarNote: Action 1 (quiz starts) → Action 2 (we arrive) → Now. Action 1 takes 'had + V3'; Action 2 takes Past Simple.

contrastExample.incorrectText: When we reached the hall, the quiz already began.
contrastExample.correctText: When we reached the hall, the quiz had already begun.
contrastExample.reason: Use 'had + V3' ('had begun') to make clear which past action occurred first.

teachingSequence.title: Past Simple vs Present Perfect
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Finished yesterday ('V2') vs continuing up to now ('has/have + V3').
teachingSequence.explanation: Compare 'Dr. Nair taught here in 2014' (Past Simple: finished past point) with 'Dr. Nair has taught physics here for twelve years' (Present Perfect: started in the past and still true today!).

timelineData.grammarNote: 'for' measures a period (twelve years); 'since' marks a starting point (2014). Never use Present Simple ('teaches') with 'for twelve years'.

teachingSequence.title: 'For' vs 'Since' & Present Perfect Continuous
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: How do 'for' and 'since' choose between period and starting point?
teachingSequence.explanation: Both 'has taught ... for twelve years' and 'has been teaching ... since 2014' connect past to present. Remember: 'for' takes a count of time (two hours, twelve years), while 'since' takes a fixed starting point (morning, Monday, 2014).

timelineData.grammarNote: Avoid the common error 'is teaching for twelve years'—duration continuing from past to now requires Perfect or Perfect Continuous.

contrastExample.incorrectText: Dr. Nair is teaching physics here for twelve years.
contrastExample.correctText: Dr. Nair has taught physics here for twelve years.
contrastExample.reason: Present Continuous ('is teaching') cannot span a 12-year duration back into the past.

teachingSequence.title: Sequence of Tenses & Universal Truths
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: When does a past main verb NOT pull the next verb into the past?
teachingSequence.explanation: Usually, a past reporting verb ('explained', 'said') pulls the subordinate clause into past tense. HOWEVER, if the subordinate clause states a universal truth or scientific fact—like 'the earth moves round the sun'—it stays in Present Simple!

timelineData.grammarNote: Scientific truths and proverbs ('Honesty is the best policy') stay Present Simple even after 'said' or 'explained'.

contrastExample.incorrectText: Our teacher explained that the earth moved round the sun.
contrastExample.correctText: Our teacher explained that the earth moves round the sun.
contrastExample.reason: The orbit of the earth is permanently true, so Present Simple ('moves') is preserved.

teachingSequence.title: Five Ways to Express Future Time
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: 'will', 'going to', Present Progressive, Present Simple, and 'will have + V3'.
teachingSequence.explanation: Class 10 distinguishes shades of future meaning: (1) 'will + V1' for decisions/promises/predictions, (2) 'be going to' for prior intentions/clear signs, (3) Present Progressive for personal arrangements, (4) Present Simple for timetables, and (5) 'will have + V3' for completion by a future deadline.

timelineData.grammarNote: 'By 5 p.m.' signals that sorting finishes BEFORE 5 p.m., calling for 'will have + V3'.
timelineData.boardModelNote: Odisha Class X lists these as 5 Future Time expressions; Assam IX-X teaches 'will/shall + have + V3' as Future Perfect. (Note: no Class 10 PSEB book was supplied in sources.)

teachingSequence.title: Choosing 'going to' vs 'will' vs Timetable
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Look at the clue: dark clouds ('going to'), timetable ('leaves'), or deadline ('will have').
teachingSequence.explanation: Don't automatically pick 'will' for every future sentence! Look for clues: dark monsoon clouds = evidence ('It is going to rain'); fixed railway schedule = Present Simple ('The Puri Express leaves at 8 a.m.'); 'by 5 p.m.' = 'will have sorted'.

timelineData.timeLabel: Matching Future Clue to Verb Form
timelineData.grammarNote: Always read the surrounding clue—evidence, timetable, or deadline—before choosing the future verb form.

teachingSequence.title: Checking Stative & Irregular Verb Forms
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Watch out for V3 forms ('begun', 'written', 'eaten') and stative verbs.
teachingSequence.explanation: After 'had', 'has/have', or 'will have', always use the V3 past participle—'had begun' (never 'had began'), 'has written' (never 'has wrote'). And keep stative verbs ('belong', 'know', 'own') out of '-ing'.

timelineData.grammarNote: Key V3 forms: begin → began → begun; write → wrote → written; eat → ate → eaten; leave → left → left.

contrastExample.incorrectText: The quiz had already began before we arrived.
contrastExample.correctText: The quiz had already begun before we arrived.
contrastExample.reason: After 'had', use the past participle V3 ('begun'), not V2 ('began').

teachingSequence.title: Inspect Timeline Links Before Guided Lab
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Tap any word to inspect its role and verb-form note, then open Guided Practice.
teachingSequence.explanation: Tap 'reached', 'had', or 'begun' above to review how each word locks into the past timeline. Next, head to the Word Laboratory to practise Class 10 timeline repairs!

wordLabActivities.title: A. Spot the Earlier Past Verb Phrase
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap the TWO words that form the Past Perfect verb showing which event happened FIRST.

sentence.title: Lab Challenge A
sentence.rawText: Before the monsoon arrived, farmers had repaired the canals.

wordLabActivities.correctFeedback: Exact! 'had repaired' happened first, before 'the monsoon arrived'.
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Tap only the two words of the earlier past verb phrase: 'had' and 'repaired'.
wordLabActivities.hint: Which two-word verb tells what the farmers finished BEFORE the rains arrived?

wordLabActivities.title: B. Sort by Time Relationship
wordLabActivities.instruction: Place each phrase into Earlier Past, Continuing to Now, or Future Milestone.
wordLabActivities.promptText: 1. Tap a phrase card, then tap the matching timeline role:

items.explanation: 'will have finished by' marks a future deadline.
'had never seen before 2022' is earlier past.

items.text: have practised chess for three years
items.explanation: 'have practised for' spans up to now.
'is going to rain' predicts near future from signs.

wordLabActivities.completeFeedback: Clean sorting! You distinguished Past Perfect, Present Perfect, and Future forms effortlessly.
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Check the auxiliary: 'had' = Earlier Past; 'has/have' = Continuing to Now; 'will have / is going to' = Future.

wordLabActivities.title: C. Assemble a Sequence-of-Tenses Sentence
wordLabActivities.instruction: Arrange the tiles to show a past report of a universal scientific truth.
wordLabActivities.promptContext: Keep the scientific truth in Present Simple!
wordLabActivities.predicateText: proved that the earth revolves round the sun.
wordLabActivities.correctFeedback: Exact! 'proved' is Past Simple, while 'revolves' stays Present Simple because it is an enduring scientific truth.
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Begin with 'Galileo proved', then 'that the earth revolves round the sun.'

wordLabActivities.title: D. Compare Future Time Expressions
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap at least two future forms to see how meaning shifts between prediction, fixed plan, and timetable.

options.meaningEffect: Presents the opening as a fixed official timetable.

wordLabActivities.takeaway: English expresses future time in multiple accurate ways depending on whether you mean a timetable, plan, or announcement.

wordLabActivities.title: E. Choose Between Past Simple & Present Perfect
wordLabActivities.instruction: Select the verb form that fits the time phrase 'since last Monday'.
wordLabActivities.sentenceAfterBlank: over two hundred science books since last Monday.

options.feedback: Past Simple ('catalogued') cuts the event off in the past and does not pair naturally with 'since last Monday'.
Exact! 'since last Monday' connects that starting day right up to now, calling for Present Perfect ('has catalogued').
Never combine 'will' with a past '-ed' form, and 'since last Monday' runs from the past up to now.

wordLabActivities.title: F. Repair the Archive Tense Clash
wordLabActivities.instruction: Inspect this flawed archive entry and select the accurate diagnosis.
wordLabActivities.brokenSentence: When we reached the station, the train already left ten minutes ago.
wordLabActivities.repairedSentence: When we reached the station, the train had already left.
wordLabActivities.question: Why must 'already left' become 'had already left' here?

options.label: The train leaving happened earlier than our past arrival ('reached'), requiring Past Perfect ('had left').
options.feedback: Spot on! Earlier of two past events uses Past Perfect ('had left'), not Past Simple.

options.label: It should be 'is leaving' because trains follow a daily timetable.
options.feedback: Look at 'reached': this reports a specific past incident, not a general timetable.

options.label: It should be 'has left' to connect with our past arrival.
options.feedback: To step further back from a Past Simple anchor ('reached'), use Past Perfect ('had left'), not Present Perfect.

independentPractice.cueText: Tap the time clue showing which deadline comes first, then select the matching verb.
independentPractice.title: Challenge 1: Future Deadline Mastery
independentPractice.instruction: Identify the deadline clue, then choose the accurate future verb form.
independentPractice.targetPrompt: Step 1: Tap the two words setting the future deadline

sentence.title: Independent Check 1
sentence.rawText: By 2030, Indian scientists [?] solar sensors across every campus.

structureSummary.predicateText: will have installed solar sensors across every campus

independentPractice.imperativeQuestion: Step 2: Which verb form expresses completion before 2030?

imperativeOptions.label: have installed
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'have installed' is Present Perfect (up to now), whereas 2030 lies in the future.

imperativeOptions.label: will have installed
imperativeOptions.feedback: Exact! 'By + future year' pairs with 'will have + V3' to show completion by that deadline.

imperativeOptions.label: installed
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'installed' puts the event in the past, not by 2030.

independentPractice.successFeedback: Clean match between 'By 2030' and 'will have installed'.
independentPractice.retrySubjectFeedback: Tap 'By' and '2030' at the start of the sentence.

independentPractice.cueText: Notice the dark monsoon clouds—present evidence points to what is about to happen.
independentPractice.title: Challenge 2: Evidence-Based Future Prediction
independentPractice.instruction: Pick the most natural future-time expression.

sentence.title: Independent Check 2
sentence.rawText: Look at those dark monsoon clouds! It _____ soon.

independentPractice.imperativeQuestion: Which form best fits visible present evidence?

imperativeOptions.label: is going to rain
imperativeOptions.feedback: Spot on! Odisha Class X teaches 'be going to + V1' for predictions backed by visible present evidence (dark clouds).

imperativeOptions.label: rained
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'rained' is Past Simple, whereas 'soon' points to the near future.

imperativeOptions.label: has rained
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'has rained' describes already-fallen rain, not clouds about to pour soon.

independentPractice.successFeedback: 'is going to rain' captures prediction from present evidence.

independentPractice.title: Challenge 3: Unfamiliar Sentence Audit
independentPractice.instruction: Evaluate which sentence obeys both Earlier Past and Irregular V3 rules.

structureSummary.predicateText: reminded us that honesty brings lasting respect

imperativeOptions.label: By the time Arjun arrived, Mira had already wrote the notice.
The speaker reminded us that honesty brings lasting respect.
imperativeOptions.feedback: Accurate! 'reminded' is Past Simple, while the timeless moral truth stays in Present Simple ('brings').

imperativeOptions.label: Our science club is having twenty microscopes since 2020.

completionSummary.headline: Archive Timeline Verified! Mission 2 Complete!
completionSummary.celebrationMessage: You helped Mira, Arjun, and Gyan restore every Class 10 archive record across Past, Present, and Future!
learnedPoints: Earlier of two past actions takes Past Perfect ('had + V3'); duration continuing to now with 'for/since' takes Present Perfect / Perfect Continuous.
Under Sequence of Tenses, universal truths and scientific laws remain in Present Simple even after a past reporting verb.
English expresses future time using 'will', 'be going to' (evidence/intent), Present Progressive (plans), Present Simple (timetables), and 'will have + V3' (deadlines).
repairedMessages: When we reached the hall, the quiz had already begun.
Dr. Nair has taught physics here for twelve years.
Our teacher explained that the earth moves round the sun.
By 5 p.m., the volunteers will have sorted all the books.
